blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Define specialisation at a national level, and trace how a country's resources lead it to concentrate production on particular goods and services.

blocks.heading: The definition and its basis
blocks.text: Specialisation at a national level is where a country concentrates its resources on producing a narrow range of goods and services, and trades the surplus for the other goods its people want. The basis, in broad terms, is superior resource allocation and cheaper production methods: a country tends to specialise where its land, climate, workers' skills or equipment let it produce at a lower cost per unit than its trading partners. Namibia's fish processing at Walvis Bay grows from a resource the country holds in strength; Vietnam's highland coffee grows where the crop suits the land. Each country puts its resources where they produce most.

blocks.heading: How the basis works
blocks.text: Start from the country's resources. Where a country holds a resource in strength - a deep-water port, a dry climate, skilled workers - production built on that resource tends to need fewer inputs per unit, so the cost per unit tends to fall. Because the country can produce these goods cheaply, land, labour and capital move towards them and away from goods that other countries produce more cheaply. The surplus is then traded: what the country makes best is exchanged for what it has decided not to make, and the total available to its consumers tends to rise.

blocks.heading: The idea in figures
blocks.text: A processing line at Walvis Bay with 60 workers packs 9 600 cartons of fish a day, 160 cartons for each worker; a general food workshop with the same 60 workers packs 4 200 cartons, 70 cartons each. The port-side line's cost per carton sits lower because its workers produce more in a day. In Vietnam, highland farmers harvest 2.4 tonnes of coffee a hectare where lowland farms harvest 1.5 tonnes, so the highlands give more coffee from each hectare. Each country produces where its resources work hardest and trades for the rest.

blocks.heading: Connections
blocks.text: The opportunity cost of concentrating on one range of goods is the ground of topic 1.4, and the trade that specialisation leads to is examined in topic 6.2.
